strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem in mechanistic interpretability: whether causal interventions produce unfaithful out-of-distribution representations
Strong empirical diagnosis showing divergence is common across multiple methods (mean difference patching, SAEs, DAS) using appropriate Earth Mover's Distance metrics
Clear conceptual framework distinguishing 'harmless' divergences (in null-space or within decision boundaries) from 'pernicious' divergences (hidden pathways, dormant behaviors)
Concrete, well-worked examples in Sections 4.2.1-4.2.2 precisely illustrating how patching can activate silent ReLUs and cause context-dependent behavioral changes
Well-structured presentation with effective visualizations (particularly Figures 1-2) and logical progression from diagnosis to proposed solution
Provides practical recommendations for practitioners including ReLU-pattern audits and context-sensitive testing
weaknesses: Critical limitation: The proposed CL loss is only evaluated on synthetic tasks with simple structure (2D feature space + 64 noise dimensions); no validation on real models where these issues matter most
Explicitly fails to deliver a reliable method for classifying pernicious divergences in practice—authors acknowledge this as 'a remaining gap,' but it undermines the framework's practical utility
Theoretical examples use extremely small, constructed networks; no empirical characterization of how frequently pathological cases (hidden pathways, dormant behaviors) actually occur in real models

Incomplete treatment of null-space divergence: the paper acknowledges the behavioral null-space is 'difficult to define in practice,' yet this is where harmless divergences occur, creating a practical circularity

Weak evaluation of the proposed solution: OOD improvements are modest (~2% in Figure 3d), only on synthetic tasks, with no ablations on the CL loss modification or comparisons to simpler projection-based approaches

Experimental design inconsistencies: different layers selected for different methods (layer 10 vs 25), and the paper notes their main EMD metric 'did not necessarily correlate with subjective interpretation of divergence'
Unclear gap between diagnosis and impact: no evidence that these problems are common enough to warrant the proposed solutions, and no clear guidance on adjusting existing workflows

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored assumption in mechanistic interpretability—the faithfulness of OOD intervened representations
Clear theoretical framework distinguishing harmless divergences (null-space, within-boundary covariance) from pernicious ones (hidden pathways, dormant behaviors) with concrete synthetic examples
Empirically demonstrates that divergent representations occur across multiple intervention methods (MDVP, SAE, DAS) using systematic Earth Mover's Distance measurements
Comprehensive multi-faceted approach combining empirical evidence, theoretical analysis, and proposed mitigation
Well-detailed appendix supporting reproducibility with experimental specifications and hyperparameter searches
weaknesses: Critical gap: proposed CL loss validated only on synthetic 2D feature data with trivial structure (grid + Gaussian noise), not on real language models or actual mechanistic interpretability questions, severely limiting practical applicability

Conflates divergence with harm—Section 3 demonstrates divergence exists but provides no evidence it actually causes incorrect mechanistic conclusions; no case studies showing real interpretability findings compromised by divergence

Incremental technical contribution: CL loss modification (averaging m > 1 vector labels, per-dimension application) is straightforward extension of Grant (2025); solution explicitly framed as 'a step towards' rather than solving the problem

Weak theoretical analysis: 'behaviorally binary subspace' is overly restrictive; identifying full behavioral null-space acknowledged as impractical; no formal characterization of when divergences become harmful (depends on unformalized mechanistic claims)

Synthetic experiments are unrealistic: 2D structured features, 128-hidden-unit MLPs, 10-class problems far from real transformers; OOD evaluation (Dense vs Sparse partitions) is artificial; Figure 4 improvements are modest without baselines or significance testing
No real-world validation: absence of experiments on actual language models, real circuits (e.g., IOI), or demonstration that reducing divergence improves mechanistic interpretability conclusions
Missing critical comparisons: no comparison to other OOD/adversarial robustness methods, manifold-preservation approaches, or ablation studies beyond hyperparameter sensitivity
Metric justification lacking: EMD choice for divergence quantification not justified; IIA (accuracy on intervened behavior) doesn't directly measure correctness of mechanistic claims
Claim overstatement: title 'common phenomenon' supported only by PCA visualization and EMD distances looking different, not by evidence this commonly affects interpretability practice
Practical guidance insufficient: authors resort to vague recommendations ('collect sufficiently large evaluation datasets') rather than concrete actionable insights for practitioners

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem in mechanistic interpretability—the reliability of causal interventions when they produce out-of-distribution representations

Provides a clear theoretical framework distinguishing 'harmless' divergences (null-space, within-boundary covariance) from 'pernicious' ones (hidden pathways, dormant behaviors) with formal definitions and rigorous mathematical treatment
Convincing empirical demonstration across multiple intervention methods (mean difference patching, SAEs, DAS) using Earth Mover's Distance as a principled divergence metric
Well-constructed synthetic examples in Section 4.2 that clearly illustrate how off-manifold interventions can activate hidden pathways and trigger dormant behaviors
Transparent acknowledgment of limitations regarding practical classification of pernicious divergences and confinement of the proposed solution to synthetic settings
Comprehensive positioning relative to related work on causal scrubbing, circuit completeness, and manifold-constrained approaches
weaknesses: Proposed CL loss solution only validated on synthetic tasks with 2 causal dimensions—no experiments demonstrating effectiveness on real models despite showing divergence in LLaMA (Section 3)
Critical limitation acknowledged but unresolved: no reliable method for classifying pernicious divergences in practice, severely limiting practical applicability of insights

Unclear practical guidance: concludes 'any divergence outside null-space is potentially pernicious' but offers only vague remedy (collect larger datasets), providing little actionable direction for practitioners
Theoretical analysis of pernicious divergence relies on hand-crafted synthetic examples—frequency and prevalence in realistic models remains unclear
Methodological contribution is incremental: CL loss is adapted from Grant (2025) with engineering choices (averaging CL vectors, per-subspace application) rather than novel algorithmic insights
Missing empirical comparisons to related manifold-constrained approaches (Verma et al., Tsiourvas et al.) mentioned in related work; only theoretical advantages claimed
ReLU-specific technical definitions (Section 4.2) lack generalization to other activation functions; dormant behavioral changes example depends on specific architectural setup
High variance in hyperparameter search (Figures 5-10) and limited OOD evaluation (specific Dense/Sparse partition) without robustness analysis or ablation studies
Notation and presentation could be clearer (e.g., bold tildes in Section 4.1, connection between schematic and visualization in Figure 1(b))

strengths: Addresses an important and under-examined assumption in mechanistic interpretability with clear practical relevance
Provides elegant theoretical contribution: Theorem A.2 proving coordinate patching guarantees divergence for most manifold geometries
Comprehensive empirical evidence that divergence occurs across multiple causal intervention methods (mean difference patching, SAEs, DAS)
Clear formalization of behavioral null-space and principled distinction between harmless and pernicious divergences with concrete examples
Proposes a concrete mitigation approach (CL loss) with validation on both real LLM experiments and synthetic tasks
Honest acknowledgment of limitations and deference of incomplete aspects to future work strengthens credibility
weaknesses: Critical gap: paper demonstrates divergence is common but fails to show it actually causes incorrect mechanistic conclusions in real models; all pernicious cases are synthetic examples
Proposed mitigation is acknowledged as incomplete—minimizing divergence magnitude doesn't guarantee elimination of hidden pathways, only reduces risk surface
Modified CL loss (L'_CL) only tested on synthetic data with known causal structure; real LLM experiments lack validation that improved EMD yields more reliable mechanistic claims

Harmlessness is correctly identified as claim-dependent but no principled method provided to determine harmful divergence for specific claims; Algorithm 1 only approximates and is not guaranteed successful
Practical guidance for practitioners remains vague, deferring concrete solutions to future work

Methodological concerns: choice of layers for visualization appears arbitrary; acknowledged lack of correlation between EMD metric and subjective divergence interpretation; linear regression shows correlation but not causation
Behavioral null-space formalism relies on k-NN PCA heuristics for practical implementation, which may fail in high-dimensional settings or for non-linear functions
Limited scope of real experiments: only Boundless DAS with 7B LLM; had to generate synthetic data to ensure valid CL vectors, indicating practical limitations
OOD improvements modest and only demonstrated on synthetic data; no evidence CL loss improves actual mechanistic claims made via DAS
